books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A: The South grew distinct from the rest of the country. Slavery and cotton came to define Southern society, and white Southerners defended slavery as part of their way of life. Some defenders compared Northern factory workers, who could be fired when business was slow, with enslaved people, who were fed and housed by their owners. Alexis de Tocqueville, visiting in the 1830s, wrote that slavery was the main source of the South's distinctiveness.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A (Southern defense of slavery; Tocqueville on slavery as the main source of Southern distinctiveness).

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A
stem: Southern defenders compared Northern factory workers with enslaved people. What point were they making?

options.text: Northern wage labor was crueler, since fired workers went unfed
Northern factories paid higher wages than Southern plantations paid their workers
options.misconception: The defenders did not praise Northern wages; they attacked Northern labor as cruel.

options.text: Enslaved people preferred factory work to farm work
options.misconception: The defenders claimed enslaved people were cared for; they never said they wanted factory work.

options.text: Northern workers asked to be enslaved instead
options.misconception: No Northern workers asked to be enslaved; the defenders invented the comparison, not the request.

rationales.A: The defenders said Northern workers were fired when business was slow and left unfed, while enslaved people were fed and housed, so wage labor was crueler.
rationales.B: The defenders did not praise Northern wages. They attacked Northern labor as cruel.
rationales.C: The defenders claimed enslaved people were cared for. They never said they wanted factory work.
rationales.D: No Northern workers asked to be enslaved. The defenders invented the comparison, not the request.
rationales.general:
1. Find the comparison. Northern workers could be fired when business was slow; enslaved people were fed and housed.
2. Ask what it proves for the defenders. If wage workers go hungry when fired, then slavery looks kinder than free labor.
3. Name the point. The defenders turned the attack around: the North, not the South, was cruel to workers.
Background: This argument came from defenders such as George Fitzhugh, who attacked the free-labor idea itself.
Remember: a comparison argues by the standard it picks.
